title: The Guru bows to the disciple
word: The Guru bows to the disciple
hook: Bhai Gurdas marvels that Nanak bowed to Angad, making the disciple the Guru (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, milk and jasmine at Multan, and your line, room for a flower. Did you bring one gentle thing into a full room? Day seven hundred seven.

A handover at work tends to go one way. The old boss signs the papers, gives a short speech, maybe cuts a cake, and walks out the door. The new one is still, somehow, the junior. Bhai Gurdas tells a handover that runs the other way round. Near the end of his first var, after the journeys and the debates we've been following, Baba Nanak chooses the one who will carry the light after him. And then he does something that makes Bhai Gurdas marvel. Today: the Guru bows to the disciple.
screen: `A HANDOVER, THE USUAL WAY.` → `BABA NANAK CHOOSES WHO COMES NEXT.` → `A HANDOVER THE OTHER WAY ROUND.`

segments.voice: The disciple's name was Lehna. Bhai Gurdas says that while Nanak was still living, he set Lehna in the Guru's place and had the canopy held over his head, the sign of the Guru's seat. He gave him a new name, Angad. And Bhai Gurdas treats it as a wonder: the master bowing to the one he'd chosen. The bow is sung in the Guru Granth Sahib too, in the var of Satta and Balwand on Ang nine hundred sixty-six: the Guru bowed to the disciple while Nanak was still alive. The teacher the crowds turned to see at Achal bows to his own student. Bhai Gurdas pictures it as light merging into light. Nanak's light didn't go out. It wasn't handed along like a lamp passed from one hand to another, leaving the first hand empty. It merged. The same light, now in a new form. Sikhs often sum it up in a phrase that turns the order upside down: the Guru became the disciple, and the disciple became the Guru. That's the hinge of today. In Sikh teaching, Guruship isn't a possession to clutch until the end. It's a light, and the one who carries it is the first to bow to it when it shines in someone else. Bhai Gurdas goes on to tell the next handings on in the same spirit: one light, a new form. And the pattern carries into Sikh life now, where Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru. Notice what the bow asks of the one who gives it. Bowing to someone you taught means trusting that what you gave them is theirs now, and might even grow in their hands in ways it never could in yours. It's a hard thing to do with a job, a recipe, a business, a family role. Nanak, in Bhai Gurdas's telling, does it with the Guru's own seat.
screen: `LEHNA IN THE GURU'S SEAT.` · `NANAK BOWS TO HIM.` · `LIGHT MERGING INTO LIGHT.` · `GURU BECOMES DISCIPLE, DISCIPLE GURU.` · then, large: `THE TEACHER BOWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn from someone younger. Use the sit to find them. A niece who knows the app you don't. A new colleague who sees an old problem fresh. A student, a kid down the street, a teenager who corrected you once and turned out to be right. Pick one person, and one thing they know that you don't. Then picture asking them, simply: show me. Notice whatever in you resists that, and let it soften a little. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with that person in mind. The bell holds the time.
The Guru bows to the disciple. Bhai Gurdas's picture of Nanak placing Angad in the Guru's seat and bowing to him: the Guru became the disciple, and the disciple became the Guru.
screen: `THE GURU BOWS TO THE DISCIPLE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the teacher bows. Today, ask someone younger to teach you one thing, and let them be the expert all the way through. Day seven hundred seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's handing on to Guru Angad, as Bhai Gurdas tells it, as one light passing into a new form, and today bow before the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru.

fork.setup: you're Baba Nanak. you've chosen the one who'll carry the light after you. what do you do?
options: keep the seat to the very end, then let it pass.
set him in the Guru's place while you live, and bow to him.
leave the choice to the crowd.
fork.reveal: Bhai Gurdas says Nanak, while living, set Lehna in the Guru's seat, named him Angad and bowed to him: the Guru became the disciple.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: light, a flame. Bhai Gurdas pictures the handover as light merging into light.

trapdoor: what you thought: a polite gesture at a retirement.
what it means: the founder sets his disciple in the Guru's seat and bows to him. the Guru becomes the disciple.
what a scholar hears: Bhai Gurdas frames it as light merging into light, one light in a new form, the way Sikhs speak of the Gurus as one light.

sources.ref: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauri 45 (Lehna installed as Angad; Nanak bows; light into light)

Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 966 (Ramkali ki Var, Satta and Balwand: the Guru bows to the disciple while Nanak lives)

notes: Var 1 pauri 45 paraphrased from memory: while living, Baba installs Lehna, waves the canopy over him, names him Angad, bows to him; 'jot samani jot vich'; Guru becomes disciple and disciple Guru. Confirm the pauri number and that the 'Guru became disciple' phrasing belongs to this pauri (it is often cited from Bhai Gurdas and from later writings).
'Bhai Gurdas goes on to tell the next handings on in the same spirit' assumes Var 1 pauris 46–48 describe the later successions this way; confirm.
No age claim is made: the practice 'learn from someone younger' comes from the outline, not from any claim about Angad's age.
Gurmukhi ਜੋਤਿ: confirm the transliteration 'joht' for the original game.

Audit (2026-10-01): the bow and the 'Guru became disciple, disciple Guru' phrase were attributed directly to Bhai Gurdas; the phrase is now 'Sikhs often sum it up', and the bow is also sourced to Satta and Balwand, Ang 966 ('gur chele rahras keeyee Nanak salamat theevadai'). 'Canopy waved' changed to 'held' (the chhatar is held; the chaur is waved). Keeper: confirm Var 1 pauri 45 has Nanak's bow and 'acharje acharj' (wonder).
